units.title: Concept of Region
units.intro: A **region** is an area with one or more shared features that make it different from neighbours. Formal (uniform) region: same climate or language. Functional: organised around a node (a city and its hinterland). Vernacular: a name people use (“the highlands”). Regions nest: a farm inside a district inside a country. Boundaries can be sharp (a coast) or fuzzy (a language mix).

cards.title: 4.1 Place Similarity and Regions
body: For many years, geographers debated whether regions exist naturally, or they are simply created by people.
Today geographers agree that people create regions.
The mixture of cultural, physical and other characteristics of places are so great that it is almost impossible to find a perfect sameness or similarity in reality.
A region defined on the basis of two or more features is called a **multiple-feature region**.
For example, a soil region is a single-feature physical region while a climate region is a multiple-feature physical region.

lessons.title: The Concept of Regions in Geography

cards.title: 4.2 The Concept of Regions in Geography
body: **Where something is located** is a fundamental question in geography.
Extent: regions have territories or areas over which physical, cultural or other similarities remain constant.
Although the boundaries of regions are indicated by lines on maps, they are rarely sharply defined.
Hierarchical Arrangement: this refers to the order of regions.

cards.title: Step by step: The concept of a region
body: **Step 1:** A region is an area of the Earth's surface that shares one or more common characteristics which make it different from surrounding areas.
**Step 2:** The characteristic can be physical (climate, relief, vegetation) or human (language, economy, administration).
**Step 3:** Every region has a location, an extent (area) and boundaries; the boundaries may be sharp (a political border) or transitional (a gradual change in climate).
**Step 4:** Geographers divide the world into regions to simplify and compare places.
**Step 5:** The size depends on the purpose: a small region like a zoba or a large one like the Sahel.
**Example:** The Eritrean coastal lowland is a region because places in it share low altitude, hot temperature and low rainfall, which make it different from the cool highland region.

cards.title: Mnemonic — L-E-B-C
body: Location, Extent, Boundary, Common characteristic: the four things that make an area a region.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When asked to define a region, always name the shared characteristic (e.g. "same climate"), otherwise the definition is incomplete.

cards.title: Step by step: Common characteristics of regions
body: **Step 1:** Regions have location: they can be placed on a map using latitude, longitude or relative position.
**Step 2:** Regions have area or extent: they cover a measurable space.
**Step 3:** Regions have boundaries, which may be clear lines or broad transition zones.
**Step 4:** Regions have homogeneity: inside the region places are similar in the chosen criterion (climate, language, farming).
**Step 5:** Functional regions instead share interaction (spatial interaction) with a centre, such as trade, transport or services.
**Example:** A climate region such as the tropical desert is defined by homogeneity (all hot and dry), while the area served by the port of Massawa is defined by interaction with the port.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Same stuff, same job"
body: homogeneity makes formal regions; interaction makes functional regions.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: If a question mentions flows, movement, a centre or services, think functional region; if it mentions one shared feature, think formal region.

cards.title: 4.4 Types of Regions
body: As patterns of spatial interaction change, new functional regions may appear and old ones may disappear.
Regions are identified and delimited using similarities.
Regions having great internal similarity, but are different from their surroundings, are called **formal or uniform regions**.
Regions showing great internal organization or connection as indicated by movement of people, commodities or information are called **nodal or functional regions**.
All types of regions remain unchanged with time.

cards.title: Step by step: Types of regions
body: **Step 1:** Formal (uniform) regions: every place shares the same feature – e.g. a climate region, a language region, a cotton-growing region.
**Step 2:** Functional (nodal) regions: areas linked to a central place (node) by movement – e.g. the market area of a town, a bus route network, a port's hinterland.
**Step 3:** Vernacular (perceptual) regions: areas that people believe exist, based on feeling or culture – e.g. "the Horn of Africa", "the Middle East".
**Step 4:** Regions can also be grouped by criterion: physical (natural) regions and human (cultural, economic, administrative) regions.
**Step 5:** Functional regions change when patterns of interaction change, so new ones appear and old ones disappear.
**Example:** Eritrea's six zobas are administrative (formal) regions; the area whose people shop in Asmara's markets is a functional region; "the Horn of Africa" is a vernacular region.

cards.title: Mnemonic — F-F-V
body: Formal = same Feature, Functional = same Flow, Vernacular = same Vision (people's view).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Give one Eritrean or African example for each type – examiners reward a correct local example more than a definition alone.

**Step 2: Contrast with functional regions.**

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Internal uniformity of physical or cultural features**.

glossary.meaning: A formal region is a non-overlapping area defined by the similarity of physical or cultural features existing in it.

tips.text: The Earth’s surface is characterised by great diversity of physical and cultural characteristics, but similarities also exist.
Regions are identified and delimited using similarities.
Only one criterion or feature may be used to define single-feature regions, while the use of two or more criteria defines multiple-feature regions.
When the criteria used are physical features, we have natural regions; when we use cultural features, we have cultural regions.
Regions having great internal similarity, but are different from their surroundings, are called formal or uniform regions.
Formal regions could be natural or cultural, single-feature or multiplefeature.
Regions showing great internal organization or connection as indicated by movement of people, commodities or information are called nodal or functional regions.
No matter how regions are defined, they all share some common characteristics like location, extent, boundary and hierarchy. Note that regions do not exist naturally.
They are spatial expression of ideas, and we can define infinite number of regions by changing or combining the criteria we use to define them.

cards.back: A formal region is a non-overlapping area defined by the similarity of physical or cultural features existing in it.
An area defined by shared characteristics.
